root.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit: Netherlands Variation
root.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 f5

parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

root.name: Philidor Defense: Steinitz Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. Bc4 Be7 4. c3

parent.name: Philidor Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. Bc4 Be7
parent.overview: Black defends e5 with the d-pawn instead of the knight, building a compact centre at the cost of space and piece mobility. Wikipedia calls it solid but passive (s1); the dark-squared bishop and sometimes the whole position can be cramped (s2, s4). The usual game is White taking space after 3.d4 or developing with 3.Bc4, and Black setting up the Hanham formation (...Nf6, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...c6, ...O-O), then freeing the position by ...exd4 or ...d5 at the right moment (s1, s4). Modern analysis finds it dynamically balanced, not just passive (s3). Strong players use it rarely; Wikipedia says no top player used it regularly as of 2017, though it has grown in rapid, blitz and bullet (s1). Move orders matter: Black must avoid several tactical pitfalls (s2, s4).

parent.name: Bishop's Opening
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 at once, eyeing f7 and discouraging ...d5, while keeping the f-pawn free for f4 and delaying the knight on g1. Unlike the Italian, White does not commit a knight to f3 on move two, so the opening is highly transpositional: after 2...Nc6 it tends to become an Italian or Vienna, after 2...Nf6 White usually plays 3.d3 (or the sharp Urusov Gambit 3.d4), and after 2...Bc5 play is symmetrical and can reach a Giuoco Piano. Theory judges it equal with best play. At master level it is a surprise weapon used to avoid Petrov preparation, not a main line.

parent.name: Three Knights Opening
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Nc3
parent.overview: A flexible, classical development move: White puts a second knight on c3 instead of choosing a bishop move. Most games go 3...Nf6, the Four Knights, which has a quiet, somewhat drawish reputation but includes sharp variations (4.Bb5 Spanish, 4.d4 Scotch). Black can avoid that with 3...Bb4, 3...g6 or 3...f5 (the Schliemann-type Gothic/Winawer), or play 3...Bc5 or 3...d6, which White meets with 4.Nxe5 or 4.d4. White's usual plans are d2-d4 to open the centre and Nd5 to dominate it. The 'Three Knights' label in play mostly covers Black's non-Nf6 sidesteps, which are rare among masters.

root.name: Sicilian Defense: Godiva Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Qb6

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Open
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4
parent.overview: After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black has developed the knight to c6 before choosing a set-up, so the root is a crossroads: Classical (5.Nc3 d6), Sveshnikov (5...e5 after ...Nf6), Four Knights (5...e6), Kalashnikov or Lowenthal (4...e5), Accelerated Dragon (4...g6) and Taimanov-type lines (s1, s2, s3). White gets a development lead and kingside space, Black gets the open c-file and a central pawn majority, so the play is unbalanced and complex (s1). The Richter-Rauzer (6.Bg5) and Sozin (6.Bc4) lead to a race where White attacks on the kingside, often castling queenside, and Black counters with ...a6, ...b5 and c-file pressure (s2). Statistics are balanced (White 47.7%, Black 47.3% in 5.6 million Lichess games, per the Chessiverse page for the Four Knights) (s3).

root.name: Englund Gambit: Soller Gambit Deferred
root.moves: 1. d4 e5 2. dxe5 Nc6 3. Nf3 f6

alternative_names: Englund Gambit Complex, Soller Gambit Deferred

parent.name: Englund Gambit
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...e5, offering the e-pawn after 2.dxe5 to avoid closed queen's-pawn positions and set tactical problems. The main line is 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Nc3, where Black regains the pawn on b2 but loses the queenside attack; the gambit relies on traps such as 6.Bc3?? Bb4! with mate threats on c1. White can simply keep the pawn and, with accurate development, retains an advantage. Strong players and engines consider it unsound for Black, and top-level players almost never choose it. It scores through quick development and traps against an unprepared opponent.

root.name: Nimzowitsch Defense: Pseudo-Spanish Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 Nc6 2. Bb5

parent.name: Nimzowitsch Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 Nc6
parent.overview: Black develops a knight on move one and invites White to build a centre, planning to undermine it with timely pieces and pawn breaks (...d5, ...e5 or ...e6). The most common reply to 2.d4 is 2...d5 with 3.exd5 Qxd5 (Scandinavian-type), 3.e5 Bf5 (French-Advance-like with a freed bishop) or the 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5 line, which is French-like in structure. Alternatively Black plays 2...e5 (Kennedy Variation), which can transpose to the Scotch, or 2...e6/2...g6 (Franco-Hiva, Pirc connection) with flexible set-ups. Kasparov and Keene wrote it has never been fully accepted as dependable, but sources agree it is far from refuted; players choose it to escape preparation and play non-standard but often French/Scandinavian-like middlegames. Roughly 2% of games per Chessable.

root.name: English Opening: Four Knights System, Nimzowitsch Variation
root.moves: 1. c4 e5 2. Nc3 Nf6 3. Nf3 Nc6 4. e4

parent.name: English Opening: King's English Variation
parent.moves: 1. c4 e5 2. Nc3 Nf6 3. Nf3 Nc6
parent.overview: After 1.c4 e5 White has what is in effect a Sicilian Defence with colours reversed and an extra tempo (s1, s2). The root is a crossroads with very different set-ups: the Botvinnik System (c4, Nc3, g3, Bg2, d3, e4, Nge2) is a slow bind on d5; the Four Knights (2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6) and 3.g3 lines give fianchetto systems; the Flohr-Mikenas-type 3.e4 and 2.Nc3 Nf6 with an early d4 are sharper (s1, s2, s4). White's recurring themes are control of d5, queenside expansion with b4 and Rb1, and the long diagonal (s2, s4). Black neutralises the extra tempo with ...d5 breaks, ...f5 or an early ...Bb4 (s2). Overall the play is flexible and manoeuvring with little forcing theory (s1, s2), though the Four Knights in this move order is described as sharper than its 1.e4 cousin (s4).
